transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-11 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Liam (Nimbus Dev Lead), Priya (Nimbus SRE), Jared (Product)

Summary: quick turnaround POC week 5. Main topics: TTFT regressions under microbursts, streaming handshake jitter, sequence-length profile shift on user queries, and kernel fallback choices. Agreed to do another synthetic microburst, share kernel benches, and send revised SOW for small dedicated buffer.

Topics:
- TTFT spikes during 95th-99th percentile bursts
- Streaming window/handshake jitter and early token path
- Sequence-length distribution shifted up after checkout flow change
- Dedicated vs hosted small reserved capacity for mitigation
- Security: KMS behavior and audit log retention (customer question)

Action items (also in metadata): see action_items field above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): all right hi everyone thanks for joining on short notice, we wanted to run through week five POC results and triage the two elevated TTFT events you saw last night. 
[00:15] Liam (Nimbus): yeah thanks, we had two big spikes around 01:12 and 03:46 UTC, average token time was fine but first-token latency shot up to 920ms on a handful of requests, which triggered our gateway retry logic and cascaded. 
[00:30] Jordan (Redwood): got it. quick clarifying q — are those bursts coming from the mobile checkout or the batch reconciliation? 
[00:38] Liam: mobile checkout, and we recently changed the fraud engine to do an extra prompt to the model which moved seqlen a bit, so our distribution now has more 400-600 token replies vs previous 150-250.
[00:55] Priya (Nimbus): yeah and note, we only see it when traffic hits multiple regions, not isolated to one AZ, so feels like pathing + microburst queueing rather than model quality. 
[01:10] Jordan: okay that aligns with the traces — some tokenization overhead plus KV cache miss for the first request after an idle period. we pulled the flamegraph and saw a hot spot in the attention kernel for long sequences — likely L2 thrash on the NVLink path.
[01:30] Carlos (Redwood): (interrupting) also FWIW the streaming handshake added 80-120ms on the control plane call in your config because you're using per-request auth, which our streaming fastpath bypass requires slightly different cookie/ttl settings.
[01:46] Maya: can you explain that a bit more, carlos? customer-facing: what should they change here? 
[01:52] Carlos: sure, the streamed websocket path expects an early auth token exchange. your setup is doing full SAML exchange on each socket reattach which is adding jitter when the client reconnects mid-response. swapping to short-lived bearer tokens or reusing the session token for 30s reduces that overhead.
[02:08] Priya: hmm we use our SSO provider's default 1-minute sessions; switching to short-lived tokens may be possible but needs sign-off. also, audit/logging around that is a compliance ask — we can't lose traceability.
[02:20] Maya: totally — that's a common constraint, we can recommend a pattern where the app uses short-lived tokens for the streaming handshake while keeping SAML for initial sign-in; we can document the audit mapping so you still surface the SAML id.
[02:32] Jared (Nimbus): quick question on dedicated capacity — you suggested a small reserved buffer to avoid those first token microbursts. what does that look like cost-wise?
[02:40] Maya: we'll include a two-tier option in the SOW: a small reserved pool (1–2 GPUs equivalent) for steady state and a burst reserve at X% for spikes. i'll send estimated monthly and a blended per-token runway in the SOW doc.
[02:55] Liam: ok thanks, please include breakouts for streaming vs non-streaming.
[03:02] Jordan: on the kernel side, we ran comparative benches between q8_0 and q4_1 quant modes and different attention kernels — for long sequences q4_1 with our tiled attention reduced median by ~12% but the 95th didn't move much because of memory-copy overhead.
[03:22] Priya: are you recommending a fallback kernel for the 95th? we don't want oscillation between kernels mid-flight.
[03:28] Jordan: yes — recommend fixed kernel selection per request class. if sequence length > 380 and token budget > 450 we pin to tiled attention + prefetch path; otherwise use streaming-optimized kernel. we also suggest a hedging policy: if the first-token exceeds 420ms, kick a small second request on a lower-latency model variant and discard the slower one.
[03:50] Liam: hedging sounds ok but adds cost — we need to quantify how often it'll fire.
[03:56] Carlos: we can add sampling to estimate the expected hedges. in your last 48h test it would have fired on 0.9% of requests but avoided 60% of retry cascades.
[04:10] Maya: solid. that's actionable: jordan to put numbers in the matrix, maya to send SOW, liam to run the synthetic microburst.
[04:20] Jared: about the microburst, what's the recommended synthetic pattern? we did a 2-minute 1k rps before and it didn't fully reproduce the ttft spike.
[04:29] Jordan: do 3 phases: warm-up at 250rps 10m, then a 5m ramp to 1200rps with 200ms inter-arrival jitter, then a 10m sustain at 800rps. make sure you include the real sequence length distribution—especially the new 400–600 token tail.
[04:48] Priya: we'll run that Friday; can you provide a k6 script or a yaml config?
[04:54] Jordan: yes, i'll upload the K6 script to the shared folder and annotate the headers.
[05:00] Maya: switching to security Qs — you asked about KMS and key rotation, priya. can you restate current constraint?
[05:08] Priya: we require customer-managed keys with rotation controls and audit logs that show which model version accessed a key. also retention for 1 year in our audit store.
[05:17] Maya: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations and we can provide HSM-backed KMS in private deployments. for hosted we offer envelope encryption with AWS KMS and log exports to your SIEM — we can map key identifiers to model IDs in the audit.
[05:33] Liam: any impact to latency when using CMK vs Redwood-managed? we've seen a 40–60ms delta elsewhere.
[05:40] Carlos: typically it's a one-time decrypt during model load and per-request envelope operations are cheap; worst case initial handshake adds 30–80ms. we'd instrument that in the bench.
[05:52] Jared: ok thanks. 
[06:00] (brief pause, background noise)
[06:20] Liam: i want to call out something — after we toggled prompt caching off the other night, the 95th improved but the 50th regressed a little. what's the tradeoff there?
[06:32] Jordan: that sounds like cache contention; when prompt cache is on, it helps for repeat prefixes but evicts other entries leading to evicted KV cache on long sequences. for your profile with more longer replies, we might recommend selective prefix caching and aggressive TTL only for short transactional prompts.
[06:50] Priya: so a hybrid cache policy? we'll need config knobs.
[06:56] Jordan: yes, we'll propose configs: TTLs, max-entries per prefix length bracket, and an adaptive evictor favoring longer sequence keepers during peak windows.
[07:10] Maya: Jordan, can you also call out any risky changes that could cause instability? customers always worry about toggling cache in prod.
[07:18] Jordan: sure — the main risk is mass KV deserialization if we change stride size; that's why we recommend canary toggles at 5% then 20%.
[07:26] Liam: can you also annotate the bench with expected rollback steps? that's helpful for our SRE runbook.
[07:32] Jordan: will do.
[07:36] Carlos: quick note on sequence-length driven kernel selection — we can do model-profiling at load-time to estimate memory working set and choose kernel variants, but that requires a slightly longer cold start (10–15s) when a new model version is pinned.
[07:50] Priya: that might be OK for background loads but not for autoscaling spikes where new hosts come up fast.
[07:57] Maya: good point — we can recommend warm pool + pre-warming for autoscale events. maybe in dedicated you can keep a 1-node warm pool that preloads the model.
[08:07] Liam: what's the cost delta for keeping warm pool?
[08:10] Maya: small — roughly 6–8% of the reserved pool bill; we'll surface that in the pricing addendum.
[08:18] Jared: i'd like to see a cost/benefit chart of warm pool vs hedging cost vs increased retries.
[08:24] Maya: noted, will include.
[08:28] (minute marker)
[09:10] Priya: on the streaming handshake again — will toggling to short-lived tokens affect compliance logs? we need to ensure the audit contains the original SAML assertion or at least the SAML id mapping.
[09:22] Carlos: yes we'll log the mapping server-side and attach it to each stream session id so your SIEM still receives the identity chain.
[09:30] Liam: ok that should work.
[09:36] Jordan: moving on to model variants — we ran a small test with a lighter decoder variant (smaller context window) for very short responses and it reduced ttft by 130ms on median but for longer sequences it lost quality. so suggestion: route by intent classifier: short-form answers to small variant, long conversational flows to full model.
[09:58] Jared: that's interesting — we do have an intent classifier before calls, but it's probabilistic ~92% accuracy. will that cause misroutes?
[10:06] Jordan: if you have misroutes, we can do step-down fallback: if the small variant starts producing low-likelihood tokens, we can transparently re-run on the full model while streaming partials; tradeoff is extra compute and slight latency but avoids user-visible hallucinations.
[10:20] Priya: can we set thresholds for that behavior? 
[10:24] Jordan: yes, we expose a per-route confidence threshold.
[10:28] Liam: about the hedging policy — what model variant would you pick as the hedged request? cheaper one or a more conservative low-latency variant?
[10:36] Jordan: usually a lower-latency simpler model as the hedged request; it's cheaper and often returns fast enough to avoid retries. the matrix will recommend choices based on your quality tolerance.
[10:48] Maya: okay we're approaching the last chunk here — let's recap decisions and owners.
[10:55] Maya: decision 1: run the synthetic microburst with new seqlen distribution (liam). decision 2: Jordan to finalize kernel selection guidance and hedging thresholds. decision 3: Maya to send SOW and dedicated buffer pricing. decision 4: Priya to confirm KMS audit mapping feasibility.
[11:16] Liam: timeline on SOW? we want to sign by end of month.
[11:20] Maya: i'll send the draft tomorrow (2027-03-12) and we can iterate — target signature week of 2027-03-22.
[11:28] Jared: if we sign, what's the expected ramp time to dedicated buffer?
[11:33] Maya: about 5 business days for small pool provisioning plus any private networking peering time. if you need VPC peering that can add a week.
[11:42] Priya: and SLA? 
[11:44] Maya: dedicated comes with an SLA for latency and uptime; i'll include the SLO numbers in the SOW.
[11:50] (few seconds of crosstalk)
[12:05] Jordan: one more technical ask — can we capture a short set of traces when you run the microburst that includes tcpdump and application logs? the packet level helps us see NVLink stalls.
[12:16] Liam: yes we'll capture tcpdump, k8s pod logs, and our gateway traces — is there a preferred format?
[12:23] Jordan: pcap + JSON logs is perfect. we'll annotate exactly which endpoints to capture in the k6 script.
[12:30] Maya: great — anything else from you team?
[12:35] Priya: just one last: retention for logs in your hosted offering — how long can we keep trace exports without extra cost?
[12:42] Carlos: default is 30 days; we can add an extended retention add-on for 1 year at a nominal fee, and export hooks to S3 for long-term.
[12:51] Priya: ok we'll discuss.
[13:00] Maya: perfect. i'll follow up with the SOW, pricing, and the kernel matrix. jordan will upload benches and k6 script. liam will run synthetic microburst and share traces by 2027-03-15.
[13:15] Liam: sounds good thanks everyone.
[13:20] Maya: thanks all, we'll reconvene next week same time unless anything urgent pops up.

(End of transcript)

Notes: transcript has occasional speaker label inconsistencies (Fireflies auto-attrib may have mis-matched some turns). Shared artifacts referenced: /shared/poc/nimbus/kernel-matrix.csv, /shared/poc/nimbus/k6-microburst.yaml, security-pack.pdf.
